guided.title: Make the clamp tests pass
guided.prompt: pytest itself needs a local install, so this exercise uses a tiny runner (`run_tests`) that works the same way: each test function uses `assert`, and the runner prints `PASS` or `FAIL` per test. Implement `clamp(x, low, high)`, which returns `low` if `x < low`, `high` if `x > high`, and `x` otherwise, so that all four tests print `PASS`.
hints: The starter function returns None, so every assertion fails. Read the tests to see the three cases.
Check the two limits with if statements, and return x when neither limit is crossed.
if x < low: return low; if x > high: return high; return x
guided.expected:
PASS test_inside_range
PASS test_below_range
PASS test_above_range
PASS test_on_the_boundary

guided.title: Average that rejects an empty list
guided.prompt: Implement `average(values)` so that it returns the mean of a non-empty list and raises `ValueError` for an empty list. The tests use the helper `raises` (a stand-in for `pytest.raises`). All three tests must print `PASS`.
hints: Two jobs: compute the mean, and refuse an empty list.
An empty list is falsy, so `if not values:` detects it; raise ValueError there.
if not values: raise ValueError(...); return sum(values) / len(values)
guided.expected:
PASS test_average_of_three
PASS test_average_of_one_value
PASS test_empty_list_is_rejected

guided.title: Write the tests
guided.prompt: The function `percent(part, whole)` is given and correct. Write three test functions named exactly `test_half`, `test_full` and `test_zero_whole_raises` and register them in the `run_tests` call. `test_half` asserts that `percent(5, 10) == 50`, `test_full` that `percent(8, 8) == 100`, and `test_zero_whole_raises` that `percent(1, 0)` raises `ZeroDivisionError` (use the `raises` helper). The output must be three PASS lines in that order.
hints: Each test is a function without parameters that contains assert statements.
For the exception test write `assert raises(ZeroDivisionError, percent, 1, 0)`.
Define the three functions, then pass them in a list to run_tests([...]).
guided.expected:
PASS test_half
PASS test_full
PASS test_zero_whole_raises

guided.title: Arrange, act, assert for a counter
guided.prompt: Implement the class `Counter`: it starts at 0, `increment()` adds 1 and `value()` returns the current count, and `reset()` sets it back to 0. The three tests (each arranges its own counter) must print `PASS`.
hints: The class needs __init__, increment, value and reset.
Store the count in an attribute set in __init__.
self.count = 0 in __init__; increment does self.count += 1; value returns self.count; reset sets it to 0.
guided.expected:
PASS test_new_counter_is_zero
PASS test_increment_adds_one
PASS test_reset_returns_to_zero

independent.title: Design tests for a shipping function (stretch)
independent.prompt: A function `shipping_cost(weight_kg)` returns 5 for weights up to and including 1 kg, 8 for weights above 1 kg up to and including 5 kg, and 12 above 5 kg. It raises `ValueError` for zero, negative or non-numeric weights. On your own computer with pytest installed, write the test file. Describe or paste the tests you would write, say why each one exists, and show the command that runs them.
independent.starter: List each test name, the input, the expected result, and the reason it is in the suite.
independent.solution: A good suite has one test per behaviour and covers the boundaries, because mistakes with `<` and `<=` live there. For example: `test_light_parcel_costs_5` (weight 0.5 gives 5), `test_exactly_one_kg_costs_5` (1 gives 5, the upper edge of the first band), `test_just_over_one_kg_costs_8` (1.01 gives 8, the first value of the second band), `test_exactly_five_kg_costs_8` (5 gives 8), `test_just_over_five_kg_costs_12` (5.01 gives 12), `test_heavy_parcel_costs_12` (20 gives 12), and error tests with `pytest.raises(ValueError)` for 0, -1 and the text "2". Each test has one assert and a name that states the behaviour, so a failure tells you which band broke. Run with `python -m pytest -q` from the folder that contains `shipping.py` and `test_shipping.py`. A weaker suite checks only one value per band and misses the boundaries.
rubric: Includes tests on both sides of each boundary (1 and 5 kg), not only one typical weight per band
Tests the error cases (zero, negative, non-numeric) with pytest.raises
Each test checks one behaviour and has a descriptive name
States the command that runs the tests, python -m pytest -q

environment.note: The bash examples need pytest on your own computer (pip install pytest in a virtual environment) and are shown read-only in the browser, with the output captured from a real run. Run them in an empty folder: they create small modules and test files there. The graded exercises use a tiny assert-based runner that works in the browser; write the pytest version of your tests locally and compare.

checks.question: Which function does pytest run automatically?
checks.explanation: Both the file name (test_*.py) and the function name (test*) must match. A test function in helpers.py is not collected because of the file name, and check_total or verify_total do not start with test.

checks.question: What does this test do? `def test_x(): assert 0.1 + 0.2 == 0.3`
checks.explanation: Binary floating point cannot store 0.1 and 0.2 exactly, so the sum is slightly above 0.3 and the assertion fails. Compare floats with pytest.approx or round them.

checks.question: A test contains `with pytest.raises(ValueError): int("12")`. What is the result?
options: Fail, because no ValueError was raised (DID NOT RAISE)
Pass, because ValueError is a built-in
Error, because int is not allowed
checks.explanation: pytest.raises passes only when the block raises the stated exception. int('12') succeeds, so the test fails with DID NOT RAISE.

checks.question: What does `assert (x > 0, "x must be positive")` do?
options: Fails when x <= 0 with the message
Always passes, because a non-empty tuple is truthy
checks.explanation: The parentheses create a tuple with two items, and a non-empty tuple is always truthy. Write assert x > 0, "x must be positive" instead.

checks.question: Your suite prints `.F.` and exits. What does the exit status tell a build server?
options: Non-zero, because at least one test failed
Nothing, since it only reads the dots
checks.explanation: pytest exits with 0 only when all collected tests pass. A single failure gives a non-zero status, which is how automated builds block a change.
